```{r, include = FALSE}
# X-13ARIMA-SEATS (package seasonal) runs the TRAMO-type regARIMA models
# when RJDemetra is not installed.
has_x13 <- requireNamespace("seasonal", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_x13,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5)
```

The OECD publishes a composite leading indicator (CLI) for Indonesia,
together with its reference series (monthly GDP) and its seven
components. For four components the OECD also publishes the original
series: share prices, the call-money rate, the rupiah exchange rate and
consumer confidence. rcli ships these series, downloaded from the OECD
SDMX interface, in `inst/extdata/oecd-idn/`, one CSV file per indicator,
as statistical offices publish them. This vignette builds a CLI from them
with `oecd_spec()` in the nine steps of rcli, twice: first against the
deviation cycle of GDP (the OECD's own reference), then against the cycle
of the annual GDP growth rate. The last section repeats the steps in the
graphical interface.

# Part A. Reference: the deviation cycle of GDP

## Step 1. Data

```{r data}
library(rcli)
dir <- system.file("extdata", "oecd-idn", package = "rcli")
files <- file.path(dir, c("gdp.csv", "share_prices.csv",
                          "call_money_rate.csv", "rupiah_per_usd.csv",
                          "consumer_confidence.csv"))
series <- read_cli_series(files)
vapply(series, attr, "", "frequency")
readLines(file.path(dir, "SOURCE.txt"))[1]
```

GDP is quarterly and the candidates are monthly. `cli_align()` brings GDP
to months with the Denton-Cholette method, which keeps the quarterly
totals, as the OECD does with its monthly GDP reference. The interest
rate is a monthly average.

```{r align}
x <- cli_align(series, type = c(gdp = "flow", call_money_rate = "average"),
               reference = "gdp")
attr(x, "alignment")
```

## Step 2. Candidates and their economic rationale

The OECD requires an economic rationale for each component and sets its
direction from it. Share prices and consumer confidence are
procyclical; a higher interest rate and a weaker rupiah (more rupiah per
dollar) come before slower growth, so both are inverted.

```{r candidates}
meta <- data.frame(
  name = c("share_prices", "call_money_rate", "rupiah_per_usd",
           "consumer_confidence"),
  rationale = c("expectations", "prime_mover", "prime_mover",
                "expectations"),
  sign = c(1, -1, -1, 1))
cand <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp", meta = meta)
cand
```

## Step 3. The OECD specification

`oecd_spec()` sets every step as in the OECD system: TRAMO-type outliers
with two months of forecasts, the log/level test, the double
Hodrick-Prescott filter (12 to 120 months), Bry-Boschan turning points,
the median-lead classification with cyclical conformity, lag-shifting,
chained average log growth and an amplitude matched by standard
deviations. With these settings rcli reproduces the published CLI of
Indonesia from its seven components (see section 8 of `vignette("rcli")`).

```{r spec}
spec <- oecd_spec()
spec
```

## Step 4. Cycles

```{r cycles}
cyc <- cli_cycles(cand, spec)
cyc$gdp@steps
```

The OECD's own reference cycle is in `oecd_cli.csv`. The GDP cycle that
rcli extracts from quarterly GDP follows it closely:

```{r reference}
oecd <- read_cli_data(file.path(dir, "oecd_cli.csv"))
ref <- stats::ts.intersect(rcli = cyc$gdp@normalised,
                           oecd = oecd[, "reference_normalised"])
cor(ref[stats::complete.cases(ref), ])[1, 2]
```

## Step 5. Turning points

```{r turning-points}
tps <- cli_turning_points(cyc, spec)
as.data.frame(tps$gdp)[, c("period", "type")]
```

## Step 6. Classification

```{r assess}
a <- cli_assess(cand, spec, cyc)
as.data.frame(a)[, c("name", "class", "median_lead", "n_matched",
                     "extra", "reasons")]
```

Only the interest rate passes the OECD rule with cyclical conformity: the
other three lead too, but they have too many extra turning points.

## Step 7. Composite

`cli_build()` keeps the leading candidates, shifts them so that their
median leads align and chains their average growth. Because only one
candidate leads, the composite of the four components is built with
`cli_composite()` from the inverted cycles that `cli_build()` returns.

```{r build}
res <- cli_build(cand, spec)
leaders(res)
cy <- cycles(res)
cli4 <- cli_composite(cy, meta$name, spec, cy$gdp)
cli4
both <- stats::ts.intersect(rcli = cli4@cycle,
                            oecd = oecd[, "cli_normalised"])
cor(both[stats::complete.cases(both), ])[1, 2]
```

The OECD CLI uses seven components, three of which (producer prices,
production of non-metallic products and tourism) are not published as
original series, so the composite of four follows it only roughly.

## Step 8. Validation

`cli_validate()` and `cli_quality()` judge the composite against the GDP
cycle:

```{r validate}
val <- cli_validate(cli4, cy$gdp, spec)
cli_quality(val, spec)
```

## Step 9. Presentation

The three OECD forms: the amplitude-adjusted CLI, the trend-restored CLI
and its 12-month rate of change.

```{r presentation}
pres <- cli_presentation(res, cli4)
tail(pres)
```

```{r plot}
a2 <- stats::ts.intersect(rcli = cli4@index,
                          oecd = oecd[, "cli_amplitude_adjusted"])
ok <- stats::time(a2)[stats::complete.cases(a2)]
a2 <- stats::window(a2, start = min(ok), end = max(ok))
plot(a2[, "rcli"], ylab = "Index (trend = 100)", xlab = NULL,
     ylim = range(a2, na.rm = TRUE),
     main = "CLI of four components (rcli) and the OECD CLI")
lines(a2[, "oecd"], col = "grey50")
abline(h = 100, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("rcli, four components", "OECD, seven components"),
       col = c("black", "grey50"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

# Part B. Reference: the cycle of the annual GDP growth rate

Users often follow the growth rate of GDP rather than its deviation from
trend. The OECD serves them with the 12-month growth rate of its
trend-restored CLI (`cli_growth_rate` in `oecd_cli.csv`). In rcli the
reference itself can be a growth rate: the cycle form of step 3 turns
every series into its annual growth rate after the outlier treatment (the
BPS formula, `100 * (Y_t / Y_{t-4} - 1)`; the call-money rate, a
percentage, is given `unit = "percent"` below so that its rate is a
difference in percentage points), and
a Hodrick-Prescott smoother (no detrending) then removes the short
movements. The form is experimental: the OECD thresholds were set for
deviation cycles. Step 1 is the same as in Part A.

## Step 2. Candidates, with the unit of the interest rate

The call-money rate is a percentage: its change is read in percentage
points, not as a growth rate of the rate.

```{r candidates-growth}
meta_g <- meta
meta_g$unit <- c(NA, "percent", NA, NA)
cand_g <- cli_candidates(x, reference = "gdp", meta = meta_g)
```

## Step 3. The OECD specification with the growth-rate form

```{r spec-growth}
spec_g <- oecd_spec(form = growth_form())
spec_g
```

## Step 4. Cycles

```{r cycles-growth}
cyc_g <- cli_cycles(cand_g, spec_g)
cyc_g$gdp@steps
```

The cycle of GDP growth moves with the OECD's CLI growth rate, which
leads it by a few months as a leading indicator should:

```{r reference-growth}
gy <- oecd[, "cli_growth_rate"]
lead_cor <- function(k) {
  z <- stats::ts.intersect(stats::lag(gy, -k), cyc_g$gdp@cycle)
  cor(z[stats::complete.cases(z), ])[1, 2]
}
sapply(c(lead_0 = 0, lead_3 = 3, lead_6 = 6), lead_cor)
```

## Step 5. Turning points

The growth cycle turns more often than the deviation cycle:

```{r turning-points-growth}
tps_g <- cli_turning_points(cyc_g, spec_g)
as.data.frame(tps_g$gdp)[, c("period", "type")]
```

## Step 6. Classification

```{r assess-growth}
a_g <- cli_assess(cand_g, spec_g, cyc_g)
as.data.frame(a_g)[, c("name", "class", "median_lead", "n_matched",
                       "extra", "reasons")]
```

No candidate passes. The interest rate still leads, by half a year, but
its turning points no longer agree with those of GDP growth often enough
for the concordance test.

## Step 7. Composite

`cli_build()` finds no leader and says so; the composite of the four
growth rates is again built with `cli_composite()`.

```{r build-growth}
res_g <- cli_build(cand_g, spec_g)
leaders(res_g)
cy_g <- cycles(res_g)
cli4_g <- cli_composite(cy_g, meta$name, spec_g, cy_g$gdp)
cli4_g
both_g <- stats::ts.intersect(rcli = cli4_g@cycle, oecd = gy)
cor(both_g[stats::complete.cases(both_g), ])[1, 2]
```

The composite of the four growth rates follows the OECD's CLI growth
rate closely, although it is built from four of the seven components.

## Step 8. Validation

```{r validate-growth}
val_g <- cli_validate(cli4_g, cy_g$gdp, spec_g)
cli_quality(val_g, spec_g)
```

The composite leads the turning points of GDP growth, but its
probability of a downturn does not beat the naive forecast: the leads
are too irregular to time slowdowns.

## Step 9. Presentation

With the growth-rate form, the trend-restored series is a growth rate in
percent (the cycle plus the mean growth of GDP), and a 12-month rate of
change of a growth rate has no meaning, so it is left empty. The plot
standardises both series to compare their timing on one axis.

```{r presentation-growth}
pres_g <- cli_presentation(res_g, cli4_g)
tail(pres_g[, c("time", "amplitude_adjusted", "trend_restored")])
```

```{r plot-growth}
std <- function(z) (z - mean(z, na.rm = TRUE)) / stats::sd(z, na.rm = TRUE)
g2 <- stats::ts.intersect(rcli = cli4_g@cycle, oecd = gy)
ok <- stats::time(g2)[stats::complete.cases(g2)]
g2 <- stats::window(g2, start = min(ok), end = max(ok))
plot(std(g2[, "rcli"]), ylab = "Standardised", xlab = NULL,
     ylim = range(std(g2), na.rm = TRUE),
     main = "Growth cycle: rcli composite and the OECD CLI growth rate")
lines(std(g2[, "oecd"]), col = "grey50")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("rcli, four components", "OECD CLI growth rate"),
       col = c("black", "grey50"), lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

# The same in the graphical interface

`run_app()` opens the interface (it needs the shiny package). The files
are in the folder printed by
`system.file("extdata", "oecd-idn", package = "rcli")`.

1. **Data.** Source *Upload several files (one per indicator)*; select
   `gdp.csv`, `share_prices.csv`, `call_money_rate.csv`,
   `rupiah_per_usd.csv` and `consumer_confidence.csv`; analysis frequency
   *Monthly*; variable type of the reference series *Flow*.
2. **Candidate metadata.** Reference series `gdp`. For each candidate set
   the rationale and the direction as in step 2 (the interest rate and the
   exchange rate countercyclical) and the variable type of the interest
   rate *Average*. For Part B also set the unit of the interest rate to
   *Ratio/percent*.
3. **Specification.** Method *Exactly as the OECD*. The interface uses
   `oecd_spec()`; *Engine of the TRAMO outliers* is automatic by default
   (TRAMO through RJDemetra, otherwise X-13), as in this vignette. For Part B set *Cycle form* to
   *Growth rate (growth rate cycle)* and *Growth rate period* to
   *Annual (y-on-y)*; the interface then writes
   `oecd_spec(freq = 12, ..., form = growth_form())`.
4. Steps 4 to 8 of the interface run the cycles, turning points,
   classification, composite and validation. Automatic mode keeps the
   interest rate in Part A and finds no leader in Part B; choose the four
   components by hand for the composites above. With the OECD method the
   interface aligns the components by their median leads (OECD
   lag-shifting) also in manual mode, so its composite equals
   `cli_composite(cy, meta$name, spec, cy$gdp, shifts =
   lag_shifts(meta$name, assessment(res)))` and differs slightly from the
   unshifted composite of this vignette.
5. Step 9 builds a composite coincident index, which this vignette does
   not need. Step 10 downloads the results, the OECD forms of
   presentation of step 9 above and an R script that reproduces them with
   the same functions as this vignette.
